fred-api-setup.Rmd

FRED API Setup

Before using the dnsr package to fetch Treasury yield data, you need to set up access to the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) API.

You may not need one yet. The package ships treasury_yields, a six-year panel of real U.S. Treasury curves, and every example in vignette("dns-model-introduction", package = "dnsr") runs against it:

library(dnsr)
data(treasury_yields)
dim(treasury_yields)
#> [1] 1501   12
range(treasury_yields$Date)
#> [1] "2019-01-02" "2024-12-31"

A key is for live or longer histories.

Getting a FRED API Key

  1. Create a FRED account (free):
    • Visit https://fred.stlouisfed.org/
    • Click “Sign In” and create a free account
  2. Request an API key:
    • Once logged in, go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/api_key.html
    • Click “Request API Key”
    • Fill out a brief form explaining your use case
    • Your API key will be generated instantly
  3. Set up your API key in R:
# Option 1: Set for current R session only
Sys.setenv(fred_api_key = "your_api_key_here")

# Option 2: Add to .Renviron for permanent setup
usethis::edit_r_environ()
# In the file that opens, add this line:
# fred_api_key=your_api_key_here
# Save and restart R

Verifying Your Setup

After setting your API key, verify it works:

# Try fetching a small amount of data
test_data <- dnsr::fetch_fred_series(
  series_id = "DGS10",
  start_date = "2023-01-01",
  end_date = "2023-01-31"
)

# If successful, you should see data:
head(test_data)

API Rate Limits

FRED API has the following limits: - 120 requests per minute per IP address - No daily limit for registered users

The dnsr package typically makes 10-12 API calls when fetching a full yield curve (one per maturity), which is well within these limits.

Troubleshooting

“FRED API key not found” error

If you see this error:

Error: FRED API key not found. Set fred_api_key environment variable or pass api_key parameter.

Solution: Make sure you’ve set the environment variable. Check with:

Sys.getenv("fred_api_key")

If it returns an empty string, your key isn’t set. Use Sys.setenv() to set it.

“FRED API request failed” error

If you see this error, possible causes: 1. Invalid API key: Double-check your key is correct 2. Network issues: Verify your internet connection 3. FRED service down: Check https://fred.stlouisfed.org/ 4. Invalid series ID: Make sure the series exists

Rate limit exceeded

If you hit rate limits:

Error: FRED API request failed with status 429: Too Many Requests

Solution: both retrying and caching are built in, so neither needs to be written by hand.

Requests are retried with exponential backoff on transient failures. A 4xx response is not retried, because a rejected key or an unknown series id will not succeed on a second attempt:

# Five attempts rather than the default three
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "2020-01-01",
                                          retries = 5)

cache_dir keeps responses on disk and serves them instead of re-requesting:

yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(
  start_date = "2020-01-01",
  cache_dir = "~/.cache/dnsr-fred"
)

# A second call with the same series and dates reads from disk
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(
  start_date = "2020-01-01",
  cache_dir = "~/.cache/dnsr-fred"
)

Two properties of the cache are worth knowing. Keys cover the series id and the requested date range only, so the API key is never part of a key and is never written to disk. And a cache hit is served before the key is looked up, which means a cached corpus can be replayed with no key configured at all – useful in CI, or for making an analysis reproducible by someone who has no key of their own.

The cache never expires on its own. Delete the directory, or the file for one series, when you want fresh data; an open-ended end_date will otherwise keep returning the range you first asked for.

Security Best Practices

⚠️ Never commit your API key to version control!

  • Don’t hardcode your API key in scripts
  • Use .Renviron for permanent storage
  • Add .Renviron to your .gitignore file
  • When sharing code, provide instructions for others to set up their own keys

Loading the Package

Now that FRED API access is set up, load the package:

library(dnsr)

[Rest of vignette content continues here…]

Example: Fetching Recent Treasury Data

With your API key configured, fetching Treasury data is simple:

# Get the last 2 years of data for all maturities
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(
  start_date = Sys.Date() - 365 * 2,
  verbose = TRUE
)

# View the structure
head(yield_data)
str(yield_data)

Selecting Specific Maturities

You can also fetch only specific maturities:

# Get only 2, 5, 10, and 30-year yields
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_data(
  maturities = c("2", "5", "10", "30"),
  start_date = "2020-01-01",
  end_date = "2023-12-31",
  verbose = TRUE
)

Available maturity codes: - Short-term: "1MO", "2MO", "3MO", "6MO" - Medium-term: "1", "2", "3", "5", "7" - Long-term: "10", "20", "30"

Missing Observations

FRED emits a row for every weekday and reports market holidays as ".", which arrives as NA. Long series also have genuine multi-year holes: DGS20 has no observations before 1993, and DGS30 none between 2002 and 2006.

By default gaps are filled by carrying the last observation forward in calendar time:

# Default: gaps take the value of the most recent earlier observation
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "1990-01-01")

The direction matters more than it may appear. The frame is returned most-recent-first, so filling in row order would take each missing yield from a later date, putting information into the past that did not exist there – look-ahead bias in anything calibrated on the result.

For long histories, cap how far a value may be carried so a multi-year hole is not silently bridged:

# Carry at most 5 calendar days; wider gaps stay NA
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "1990-01-01",
                                          max_gap = 5)

# Or leave every gap alone and handle them yourself
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "1990-01-01",
                                          fill_missing = FALSE)

fit_dns_model() handles NA yields directly: maturities with no observation on a date are dropped from that date’s fit and reported as NA in the fitted matrix, and a date with fewer than three observations is listed in the result’s failures rather than silently producing a meaningless curve.

Row order

Rows are returned most-recent-first. date_order = "ascending" reverses that if a chronological frame is more convenient:

yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "2020-01-01",
                                          date_order = "ascending")

Either way, fit_dns_model() selects its window by date rather than by row position, so n_days means the same thing in both.

Data Format

The fetched data is returned as a data frame with: - First column: Date (most recent dates first) - Remaining columns: Yield values for each maturity (in decimal form) - Column names: Maturity in years (e.g., "0.25" for 3-month, "10" for 10-year)

# Example data structure:
#   Date         0.25    0.5     1       2       5       10      30
#   2023-12-31  0.0521  0.0534  0.0489  0.0452  0.0425  0.0398  0.0412
#   2023-12-29  0.0523  0.0536  0.0491  0.0454  0.0427  0.0400  0.0414
#   ...

This format is designed for direct use with the DNS model fitting functions in the package.
